analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in hospitals and protects nurses who object to unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees in June 2011 and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the 112th Congress ended, with 27 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital in the country to keep registered nurse staffing at or above fixed minimums by unit — for example, no more than four patients per nurse on a medical-surgical ward, and one nurse per patient in intensive care. Hospitals would have to post their actual staffing levels publicly, keep records auditable by regulators, and could not force nurses to work mandatory overtime to fill gaps. Nurses who believe an assignment violates the ratios or exceeds their training could refuse it without being fired or reported to licensing boards. Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted upward to cover the added costs of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would get more nursing attention per bed; and direct-care nurses, who would get enforceable staffing limits, protection from retaliation for refusing unsafe assignments, and a federal hotline and complaint process for reporting understaffing.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the number of patients each direct-care registered nurse can be assigned by unit type, from one patient per nurse in trauma and operating rooms to six in postpartum and well-baby nurseries, and forbids hospitals from averaging staffing numbers across shifts to meet the minimum.

Lets a nurse refuse an assignment she believes violates the ratios or that she is not trained to handle safely, and bars hospitals from firing, retaliating, or reporting that nurse to a state licensing board for doing so, with a right to sue for reinstatement and lost wages.

Requires hospitals to post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit where staff, patients, and the public can see them, keep three years of staffing records open to the public and to nurses' unions, and submit to federal audits.

Prohibits mandatory overtime as a way to meet the ratios, requires that only a registered nurse cover another nurse's breaks, and allows complaints to a toll-free federal hotline, backed by civil penalties up to $25,000 per knowing violation and public naming of penalized hospitals.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire enough nurses to meet the minimums and face penalties for violations; taxpayers indirectly, since Medicare payments to hospitals would be adjusted upward to cover the added costs of complying, and federal hospitals would need appropriated funds.

drawbacks.text: A ratio mandate does not create nurses. With a documented national nurse shortage, hospitals could be legally required to staff at levels the labor market cannot fill, and the bill's own findings acknowledge the rules are meant partly to fix retention problems that a staffing mandate alone may not solve.

Fixed ratios are a one-size-fits-all approach: the bill requires a national acuity tool for staffing above the minimums, but the minimums themselves apply to every hospital regardless of patient mix, local conditions, or existing state standards, though states with equivalent rules keep their own.
Medicare would cover hospitals' net additional compliance costs, meaning some of the cost of the mandate would be shifted to federal taxpayers rather than absorbed by the industry.
Rural hospitals would get four years rather than two to comply, acknowledging that small facilities face particular difficulty absorbing the added staffing requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety case is strong — the bill's own findings cite a Joint Commission report attributing nearly a quarter of unanticipated hospital patient deaths and injuries partly to inadequate registered nurse staffing — and the bill pairs the mandate with whistleblower protections that give nurses real enforcement power. The honest costs are that compliance is expensive, some of that expense passes to Medicare, and a ratio mandate cannot conjure nurses into existence during a shortage; whether fixed numbers or hospital-level flexibility better protect patients was the substance of the debate the bill never got to have.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on June 15, 2011, joined by 27 cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
Within a week both committees referred it to their Health subcommittees, which took no further action.
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals came out ahead: they avoided a federal staffing mandate, mandatory-overtime restrictions, and civil penalties for understaffing. Hospital patients and nurses, whom the bill was written for, gained nothing, and the underlying staffing problem it documented remained unaddressed by federal law.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Nurse Staffing Standards for Patient Safety and Quality Care Act of 2011.

for.name: Rep. Pete Stark
for.role: Original cosponsor and senior member, House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Was among the 11 members listed as joining the bill at introduction, giving it a co-sponsor on the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare payments.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote during the 112th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of jurisdiction over Medicare payments, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote during the 112th Congress.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.role: Hospitals and hospital associations that would bear the staffing mandate's costs
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal nurse-to-patient ratio mandates, which hospital groups argued were inflexible and costly; no formal position appears in the congressional record, so their role here reflects widely reported industry opposition to similar ratio bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would require hospitals to hire nurses up to fixed minimum ratios, restrict mandatory overtime, post staffing levels publicly, and face civil penalties of up to $25,000 per knowing violation, with Medicare payment adjustments covering some but not all added costs. Hospitals have generally fought ratio mandates on cost and flexibility grounds, and the industry's savings from the bill's death came directly out of the staffing protections patients and nurses would have gained.

Nurses would gain enforceable staffing limits, protection from retaliation for refusing unsafe assignments, access to staffing records, and a complaint hotline. Better staffing is also the mechanism through which patients would benefit, so nurses' interest in the bill ran alongside the public's.
